title: Singapore Pays Well. So Why Are Only 14% of Its Employees Engaged?
summary: Only 14% of Singapore employees are engaged, and under-35s sit at 10%. What the data says and what HR leaders can do about it.
body_markdown:
Singapore has some of the best salaries, infrastructure and job stability in Asia. It also has one of the least engaged workforces in the region.


According to Gallup's State of the Global Workplace 2026 report, only 14% of employees in Singapore are engaged at work. The Southeast Asia average is 25%. The global average is 20%. And this isn't a bad year. Singapore's engagement has hovered around this level since 2019.


If you lead HR in Singapore, that number deserves more than a slide at the next town hall.


## The numbers behind the problem


The inaugural Singapore Workplace Report 2026, published by the Singapore Institute of Directors with Gallup, puts a price on it. With 86% of the workforce not engaged, the report estimates the cost to the economy at US$73.6 billion in lost productivity every year.


The regional comparison is uncomfortable:


Country


Employees engaged at work


Philippines


39%


Thailand


34%


Indonesia


27%


Malaysia


25%


Singapore


14%


Singapore has the strongest economy on this list and the weakest engagement. Pay and stability clearly aren't doing the work many leaders assume they do.


## Your youngest employees are checking out first


The most worrying finding sits inside the average. Singapore employees under 35 report an engagement rate of just 10%, compared to 16% for those aged 35 and above. That six-point gap is nearly three times wider than the global gap between the same age groups.


These are the people you are counting on to become your next managers. Right now, nine in ten of them are not engaged.


It's tempting to blame a generation. Resist that. The same age group is far more engaged in Manila and Bangkok, which points less to age and more to how early careers are experienced in Singapore: high costs of living, intense competition for progression, and managers who are stretched themselves.


## Why disengaged employees aren't leaving


Here's the part that should worry you more than the 14%. Disengaged employees in Singapore mostly aren't quitting.


Only 42% of Singapore employees told Gallup it's a good time to find a job, compared to 64% across Southeast Asia. ADP's People at Work 2026 report found that only 15% of Singapore employees feel confident about their job security, below the Asia-Pacific average of 18%. And Morgan McKinley found nearly half of Singapore employees expect restructuring, automation or cost-cutting to affect their jobs.


So people stay. They do what's asked, they don't do more, and they wait. Attrition looks healthy on your dashboard while productivity quietly leaks away.


That's the trap. Low turnover gets read as loyalty when it is often a lack of options.


## Managers are running on empty too


"Fix your managers" is easy advice. Gallup's global data shows why it's harder than it sounds: manager engagement fell to 22% in 2025, down five points in a single year. Managers used to be more engaged than the people they led. Increasingly, they aren't.


Yet the same research shows that in best-practice organisations, 79% of managers are engaged. The gap is not inevitable. It is built, or undone, by how organisations support the people in the middle.


## What HR leaders in Singapore can do now


**1. Stop treating low attrition as good news.** Pair turnover data with engagement and sentiment data. A team with low attrition and low engagement is a risk, not a win.


**2. Listen at the moments that shape early careers.** Annual surveys miss what happens at day 30, after a first appraisal cycle, or when a young employee's manager changes. Short, regular conversations at these moments surface problems while they are still fixable.


**3. Segment by age and tenure, not just by department.** A company-wide engagement score can hide an under-35 score half its size. If you don't cut the data, you won't see it.


**4. Give managers fewer reports and clearer actions.** Managers don't need another dashboard. They need to know which two or three people on their team need a conversation this week, and what to talk about.


**5. Close the loop visibly.** The fastest way to kill engagement is to ask for feedback and do nothing. Tell people what you heard, what you are changing, and what you are not.


## The bottom line


Singapore's engagement problem isn't new, and another benefits refresh won't solve it. It needs organisations to listen more often, look harder at their youngest employees, and treat "they're not leaving" as a question rather than an answer.
